title: Levine's Conjecture (Conjecture 1.1)
context_text: Lionel Levine proposed this conjecture in the context of his hat challenge with Friedrich, later popularized by Khovanova's 2011 blog. Here $p(t)$ is the limit as $n\to\infty$ of the maximal success probability $p(t,n)$ for $t$ players each with a stack of $n$ independently colored hats who must simultaneously each pick a black hat.
paper_contribution: Proves that $p(t+1) < p(t)$ for all $t \geq 1$, establishing strict monotone decrease of the success probability, which is progress toward but does not resolve the conjecture.
paper_title: The success probability in Levine's hat problem, and independent sets in graphs

title: Conjecture 2.1
context_text: Let $B=\{0,1\}^n$ and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a family of subsets of $B$ (winning sets). In the $t$-player game each player is assigned a uniformly random point of $B$, sees the points of the other players but not her own, and then all players simultaneously name a set of $\mathcal{W}$; they succeed if every player named a set containing her own point. A strategy is a $t$-tuple $(f_1,\dots,f_t)$ with $f_i:B^{t-1}\to\mathcal{W}$, its winning set is the set of $x\in B^t$ with $x_i\in f_i(x^{-i})$ for all $i$ ($x^{-i}$ is $x$ with the $i$-th coordinate deleted), $p(t,n)$ is the maximum uniform measure of such a winning set and $p(t)=\lim_{n\to\infty}p(t,n)$. Three choices of $\mathcal{W}$: dictators $\{x:x_i=1\}$ (this is Levine's hat game: each player has a stack of $n$ random black/white hats and must point to a black hat on her own head), giving $p_{\mathrm{dict}}$; all intersecting families (sets $W$ such that any $x,y\in W$ have a coordinate $i$ with $x_i=y_i=1$), giving $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}$; and all balanced monotone families (up-sets containing exactly half of $\{0,1\}^n$), giving $p_{\mathrm{monotone}}$. Since every dictator is intersecting and every maximal intersecting family is balanced monotone, $p_{\mathrm{monotone}}(t)\ge p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t)\ge p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t)$. Levine's conjecture is that $p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$; known bounds are $0.35\le p_{\mathrm{dict}}(2)\le0.361607$ and $p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t)=\Omega(1/\log t)$, and the authors prove $p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t+1)<p_{\mathrm{dict}}(t)$ for all $t\ge1$. This conjecture is the strengthening of Levine's conjecture where winning sets are all intersecting families. It is equivalent to the graph statement $\lim_{t\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar{\alpha}(K(n)^{\square t})=0$, where $K(n)$ is the Kneser graph on $\{0,1\}^n$. Changing the order of the limits gives an uninteresting question, since for fixed $n$, $p(t,n)\to0$.
paper_title: The success probability in Levine's hat problem, and independent sets in graphs

title: Conjecture 2.6
context_text: The Kneser graph $K(n)$ has vertex set $\{0,1\}^n$, with $x\sim y$ when their supports are disjoint (no $i$ with $x_i=y_i=1$); its independent sets are exactly the intersecting families. The Hamming product $G_1\square\cdots\square G_t$ has vertex set $V(G_1)\times\cdots\times V(G_t)$, two tuples being adjacent if they differ in exactly one coordinate $i$ and are adjacent in $G_i$ there (the usual Cartesian product); $G^{\square t}$ is the $t$-fold power. $\bar{\alpha}(G)=\alpha(G)/|V(G)|$. This is a graph-theoretic restatement of the conjecture that $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t)\to0$, coming from a generalization of Levine's hat game: $t$ players each receive a uniformly random point of $\{0,1\}^n$, each sees all points but her own, and they simultaneously each name an intersecting family; they win if each named family contains her own point. An independent set of $K(n)^{\square t}$ meets every one-dimensional fiber of $(\{0,1\}^n)^t$ in an intersecting family, exactly as a winning set of a strategy does, which gives the authors' observation $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t,n)=\bar{\alpha}(K(n)^{\square t})$, where $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t,n)$ is the maximum success probability and $p_{\mathrm{intersecting}}(t)$ its limit as $n\to\infty$. Since every dictator family $\{x:x_i=1\}$ is intersecting, the conjecture implies Levine's hat conjecture (where players must name a dictator, i.e. point to a black hat in a stack of $n$ random black/white hats), which asserts that the success probability tends to $0$ as $t\to\infty$.

title: Conjecture 2.8
context_text: For a graph $G$ let $\mu$ be the uniform probability measure on $V(G)$, $\bar{\alpha}(G)=\max_I\mu(I)$ over independent sets $I$. Let $\mathcal{D}_r$ be the set of probability distributions on subsets $R\subseteq[r]$ in which every $i\in[r]$ belongs to $R$ with probability $1/2$ and all these events are positively correlated, and $\mathcal{D}=\bigcup_r\mathcal{D}_r$. Define $\alpha^*(G)=\max E_{R\sim D}\left[\max_I\mu\left(I\cap\bigcup_{i\in R}V_i\right)\right]$, the outer maximum being over $r$, $D\in\mathcal{D}_r$ and partitions $V(G)=V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_r$ (parts may be empty), the inner one over independent sets $I$ of $G$. Let $\varepsilon^*(\alpha)=\inf_{G:\,\bar{\alpha}(G)\ge\alpha}\{\bar{\alpha}(G)-\alpha^*(G)\}$. The authors show that this conjecture would imply that $\bar{\alpha}(K(n)^{\square t})$ tends to $0$ (as $t\to\infty$, after $n\to\infty$), where $K(n)$ is the Kneser graph on $\{0,1\}^n$ (vectors adjacent when their supports are disjoint) and $\square$ the Cartesian (Hamming) product, and hence Levine's conjecture that the success probability in his hat game (each of $t$ players has a stack of random black/white hats, sees all other hats and must point to a black hat on her own head; all must succeed) tends to $0$ as $t$ grows. The authors do not know whether the conjecture holds even when $D$ is the binomial distribution, or when each $V_i$ is a single vertex (which is the conjecture $\varepsilon^{**}(\alpha)>0$ about a uniformly random subset of vertices).

title: Conjecture 2.9
statement_text: $\varepsilon^{**}(\alpha) > 0$ for all $\alpha \in (0, 1/2)$. In other words, there exists a monotone non-decreasing function $\varepsilon^{**} : (0,1/2) \to (0,1/2)$ such that the following holds: if $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices with maximum independent set of size $\alpha n$, $W$ is a binomial random subset of $V(G)$, and $I_W$ is the maximal independent set contained in $W$, then $$\alpha^{**}(G) = E_W\!\left[|I_W|/n\right] \leq \alpha - \varepsilon^{**}(\alpha).$$
context_text: For a graph $G$ let $\mu$ be the uniform probability measure on $V(G)$, $\bar{\alpha}(G)=\max_I\mu(I)$ over independent sets $I$. $\alpha^{**}(G)=E_W[\max_I\mu(I\cap W)]$, where $W$ is a uniformly random subset of $V(G)$ (each vertex included independently with probability $1/2$) and $I$ ranges over independent sets of $G$; that is, $\alpha^{**}(G)$ is the expected independence number of the random induced subgraph $G[W]$ divided by $n$. $\varepsilon^{**}(\alpha)=\inf_{G:\,\bar{\alpha}(G)\ge\alpha}\{\bar{\alpha}(G)-\alpha^{**}(G)\}$; in the second formulation, $I_W$ denotes a maximum independent set of $G[W]$. This is the special case, where each part of the partition is a single vertex, of the authors' more general conjecture $\varepsilon^*(\alpha)>0$ for positively correlated random unions of parts, which would imply Levine's hat conjecture; the authors call it a fundamental problem in the study of independent sets in graphs. They prove it for $\alpha>1/4$: if $\alpha(G)=(1/4+\tau)n$ with $0<\tau<1/4$ then $\alpha^{**}(G)\le1/4+\tau-\tau^2/3$; and for regular graphs with $\alpha>1/8$: for every $\tau>0$ there is $g(\tau)>0$ such that every regular $G$ with $\alpha(G)=(1/8+\tau)n$ has $\alpha^{**}(G)\le1/8+\tau-g(\tau)$. It remains open below these thresholds. The best known upper bound, from $G(n,p)$, is $\varepsilon^{**}(\alpha)<\alpha2^{-\Omega(1/\alpha)}$.

title: Bollobás–Erdős–Tuza Conjecture (Conjecture 4.1)
statement_text: [Full statement not captured — appears in Section 4, which was not included in the PDF extraction.]
context_text: The conjecture, due to Bollobás, Erdős and Tuza, concerns bounding the size of a set of vertices that intersects every maximum-size independent set in a graph. The proof technique for the main theorem leads naturally to this problem.
paper_contribution: Provides a construction of an infinite family of graphs $G_n$ where $G_n$ has $n$ vertices, independence number at least $n/4$, and no set of fewer than $\sqrt{n}/2$ vertices intersects all maximum independent sets, yielding a bound related to the conjecture.
